title: Ezekiel 40:17–27
context: The guide brings the prophet into the outer court, with its pavement and thirty rooms. He measures the distance from the outer gate to the inner court, one hundred cubits, and then measures the north and south gates of the outer court. Each matches the east gate in its rooms, posts, arches, windows, and palm trees, each is fifty cubits long and twenty-five cubits wide, and each is reached by seven steps. Opposite each outer gate stands a gate to the inner court, again one hundred cubits away. The repeated phrase “the same as the measure” shows a single pattern for every gate.

verses.text: Then he brought me into the outer court. Behold, there were rooms and a pavement made for the court all around. Thirty rooms were on the pavement.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then he brought me into the outer court.” Arminian readers see the prophet led into a broad court with “a pavement made for the court all around” and thirty rooms on it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the purpose of the thirty rooms is not stated. Some readers connect them with gatherings or meals of worshipers, while others leave their use open, since the text does not say.

verses.text: The pavement was by the side of the gates, corresponding to the length of the gates, even the lower pavement.
verses.arminianNotes: “The pavement was by the side of the gates.” Arminian readers see the pavement running along the gates, called “the lower pavement” because the outer court was lower than the inner court.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the rising levels of the courts, reached by steps, give a sense of increasing holiness as one draws nearer to the house. Readers in both traditions share this observation.

verses.text: Then he measured the width from the forefront of the lower gate to the forefront of the inner court outside, one hundred cubits, both on the east and on the north.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then he measured the width from the forefront of the lower gate to the forefront of the inner court outside, one hundred cubits.” Arminian readers see the distance between outer and inner gates, measured on both east and north.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the number one hundred recurs throughout the vision. Many see in such round measures a sense of completeness and order, while holding that view without pressing it too far.

verses.text: He measured the length and width of the gate of the outer court which faces toward the north.
verses.arminianNotes: “He measured the length and width of the gate of the outer court which faces toward the north.” Arminian readers see the guide turning from the east gate to the north gate and beginning to measure it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the vision moves systematically around the court. The order of the tour reinforces the impression of a complete, coherent plan.

verses.text: The lodges of it were three on this side and three on that side. Its posts and its arches were the same as the measure of the first gate: its length was fifty cubits, and the width twenty-five cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: “The lodges of it were three on this side and three on that side.” Arminian readers see the north gate built just like the east gate, “the same as the measure of the first gate.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that its length is “fifty cubits, and the width twenty-five cubits,” matching verses 13 and 15. The vision repeats measurements to show uniformity in the house of God.

verses.text: Its windows, its arches, and its palm trees were the same as the measure of the gate which faces toward the east. They went up to it by seven steps. Its arches were before them.
verses.arminianNotes: “Its windows, its arches, and its palm trees were the same.” Arminian readers see the north gate matching the east gate in every detail, approached by “seven steps.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the seven steps up to the outer gates, which will be followed by eight steps to the inner gates in verse 31. Many see the ascent as picturing a drawing near to God, though the text does not explain it.

verses.text: There was a gate to the inner court facing the other gate, on the north and on the east. He measured one hundred cubits from gate to gate.
verses.arminianNotes: “There was a gate to the inner court facing the other gate.” Arminian readers see each outer gate aligned with an inner gate, “one hundred cubits from gate to gate.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the precise alignment of the gates on the north and east. The plan is orderly and symmetrical, a feature both literal and symbolic readers emphasize.

verses.text: He led me toward the south; and behold, there was a gate toward the south. He measured its posts and its arches according to these measurements.
verses.arminianNotes: “He led me toward the south; and behold, there was a gate toward the south.” Arminian readers see the guide completing the circuit of outer gates with the south gate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the phrase “according to these measurements,” which again links this gate to the pattern of the east gate. The vision presents a unified design.

verses.text: There were windows in it and in its arches all around, like the other windows: the length was fifty cubits, and the width twenty-five cubits.
verses.arminianNotes: “There were windows in it and in its arches all around.” Arminian readers see the south gate matching the others, “like the other windows,” fifty cubits long and twenty-five wide.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the repetition can feel tedious, yet it serves the vision's point. The house is measured completely, and nothing in it is left to chance.

verses.text: There were seven steps to go up to it, and its arches were before them. It had palm trees, one on this side, and another on that side, on its posts.
verses.arminianNotes: “There were seven steps to go up to it.” Arminian readers see the south gate approached like the others, with palm trees “on this side, and another on that side, on its posts.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the palm trees appear on every gate, as in verse 16. The decoration is consistent throughout, which strengthens the sense of one ordered house.

verses.text: There was a gate to the inner court toward the south. He measured one hundred cubits from gate to gate toward the south.
verses.arminianNotes: “There was a gate to the inner court toward the south.” Arminian readers see the inner south gate facing the outer south gate, again “one hundred cubits from gate to gate.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that this completes the description of the outer court. The tour now moves inward, toward greater nearness to the house itself.
